chunks: What registers are. The question: What are registers?
A register is a small, very fast storage spot that holds a fixed number of bits, such as 8, 16 or 32. There are two kinds.
Registers inside the CPU hold the values it is working on right now. Peripheral registers are how your code controls hardware such as a pin, timer, or serial port.
Each one sits at a fixed address, and each bit in it often has its own meaning.
Picture the control panel of a machine. Each register is one row on the panel. Some bits are switches you flip to make the machine do something (control bits).
Others are lamps that tell you what it is doing (status bits). Writing a 1 to a bit flips a switch. Reading a bit looks at a lamp.
A few lamps have a quirk: looking at them or touching them resets them.
Software writes go through the bus decoder into a register whose output feeds hardware; hardware can also write back into status registers, which software reads.
Registers are two-way mailboxes between code and logic.
Bit: one binary digit, 0 or 1. Peripheral register: ("How a microcontroller stores data"): a register at a fixed address that controls or reports on a hardware block.
Bit field: a group of neighboring bits that together form one setting. Mask: a number with 1 seconds at the bit positions you want to select.
volatile: a C keyword that tells the compiler a value can change on its own, so it must really read or write it each time.
An 8-bit register controls a port, and bit 5 drives an LED. The register currently holds 0b00000001.
To turn the LED on without disturbing the other bits, read the register, set bit 5 with a mask, and write it back. The mask is 0b00100000.
Combining it with OR (each result bit is 1 if it is 1 in either number) gives 0b00100001. This read, change, write sequence is called read-modify-write. That is the whole idea.
"A register is a small group of flip-flops holding a few bits.

There are CPU registers, which hold operands and the program counter, and peripheral registers, which are memory-mapped control, status and data locations that firmware reads and writes to control hardware, like setting a GPIO pin or starting a timer.
They're split into bit fields, changed with mask-and-shift read-modify-write, and declared volatile in C. Registers are the interface between software and hardware."
